article.title: US Navy Fleet Costs Surge Over Trump-Class Warships
article.summary: A new congressional report warns that US Navy fleet costs have escalated by billions due to commitments to the proposed Trump-class warships, as officials admit the ongoing Iran war is heavily straining naval capacity.

article.content_html:
Congressional Report Warns of Billions in Overruns

The US Navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has driven up the cost of its upcoming fleet by billions of dollars, according to a congressional report delivered to the US Congress. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis of the navy's 2027 shipbuilding plan reveals that previous cost projections were unrealistically low because ship designs proved far more complicated than initially anticipated.

Total shipbuilding expenses are projected to average $54bn annually in 2026 dollars over the next 30 years, marking an 18% increase over the navy's original estimates. Meanwhile, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao conceded during a Senate confirmation hearing that the ongoing conflict with Iran is actively stretching the fleet's operational capacity and creating severe strains on naval personnel and equipment.

Key Findings from the CBO Budget Analysis

  • The CBO found that total shipbuilding costs will average $54bn annually over the next 30 years, exceeding navy estimates by 18%.
  • Much of the additional expense stems from the navy's plan to purchase 15 large, heavily armed Trump-class battleships.
  • Senate appropriators proposed cutting to zero the $1bn sought by the navy for advanced procurement of the Trump-class ships this fiscal year.

Operational Strain and Pacific Deployment Gaps

The financial warning arrives as the world's largest naval force grapples with severe operational demands across global waters. Recent vulnerabilities were underscored when the return of the USS George Washington ended a rare three-month period where the United States had zero aircraft carriers operating across the entire Pacific region. Deployments have frequently exceeded 300 days while maintenance and repair schedules are routinely deferred.

Outpaced in shipbuilding by China, the US Navy intends to grow its fleet from 286 battle force ships to 381 over the coming three decades. However, budget analysts note that purchasing 15 large Trump-class battleships directly contradicts the navy's stated objective to distribute firepower across a greater number of smaller vessels, complicating both strategic goals and fiscal accountability.
